I sliced the bracket (60×20×30 mm, 0.20mm Standard process on the H2D) in both filaments. PETG roughly doubles the print time and uses about half a gram less filament.

| | PLA Basic | PETG Basic | Difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| Print time | 15 min 34 s | 32 min 28 s | **+16 min 55 s with PETG (about 2.1×)** |
| Filament | 14.18 g (4.68 m) | 13.63 g (4.53 m) | **−0.54 g with PETG (about 4% less)** |

- **Time:** Almost all of the extra time is in the walls and sparse infill, because the PETG preset limits how fast plastic can be pushed through the nozzle. Sparse infill alone takes about 7 min with PLA and about 17 min with PETG.
- **Grams:** PETG comes out slightly lighter even though it is a bit denser. The likely reason is that the PETG preset sets a lower flow ratio, so less filament is laid down in total.

Filament slot 1 is now set to **Bambu PETG Basic @BBL H2D 0.4 nozzle**, and the latest slice is the PETG one. It passed the G-code check and is ready to export or print.

I've built the coaster and saved it as `coaster.only3d.json`. It can't be sliced here because only3d's own slicer only handles one filament per plate, so the print has to go through Bambu Studio.

**What I built**
- A 90 mm × 4 mm disc in filament slot 1, the default beige PLA Basic. It sits in the middle of the plate.
- A red ring on top, in filament slot 2. I set slot 2 to Bambu PLA Basic in red (#C8102E). The ring's outside diameter is 80 mm and its inside is 70 mm, so it is 5 mm wide and 5 mm in from the edge. It is 1 mm high and sits directly on the disc's top face, which makes the coaster 5 mm tall in total.
- The ring is part of the coaster object rather than a separate object, so moving, rotating or scaling the coaster takes the ring with it.
- All sizes are adjustable parameters: `coaster_d`, `coaster_h`, `ring_w`, `ring_h` and `ring_inset`.

**Check results**
- The coaster is a closed, printable solid and fits well inside the plate.
- There is a "needs support" warning for 1178 mm² of overhang. That figure is exactly the area under the ring. Cuts across the model show the disc is solid at 2 mm and only the ring is present at 4.5 mm, so the ring rests directly on the disc. The warning is a side effect of the ring being a separate coloured body, and no supports are needed.
- The "2 separate bodies" note is expected for the same reason.

**How to print it**
1. Load red PLA into the AMS slot you want to use for colour 2.
2. Export the plate to a Bambu Studio project with `export_bambu_project {"open": true}`. That tool wasn't available in this session, so you'll need to run it from the only3d window or ask me again where it's available.
3. In Bambu Studio, map filament 1 to your beige spool and filament 2 to the red one. Leave supports off and use the 0.20 mm Standard profile on the textured PEI plate.
4. Slice and print. The first 4 mm (20 layers) print in beige, and the colour changes once for the last 5 layers of red. That keeps purge waste small. Putting red on the second nozzle would avoid it almost entirely.

I couldn't slice it, so I don't have a print time. A fully solid coaster would weigh about 33 g, which is the most it could use; with normal infill it will be less.

I've designed the coat hook in only3d. The printability check passes with no errors or warnings, and the hook needs no supports on the H2D.

## The design
A one-piece J-hook, 29 × 100 × 25 mm, about 26 g of PLA (if printed solid).

| Param | Value | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `plate_t` × `plate_h` | 5 × 100 mm | Back plate that goes against the wall |
| `width` | 25 mm | Width of the hook |
| `arm_t` | 8 mm | Thickness of the arm |
| `gap` | 18 mm | Opening for the 15 mm hanger loop (3 mm spare) |
| `lip_t` × `lip_h` | 6 × 30 mm | Up-turned tip that stops the loop sliding off |
| `gusset` | 4 mm | 45° brace in the inside corner between plate and arm |
| `hole_lo` / `hole_hi` | 60 / 88 mm | Heights of the two screw holes |

The screw holes are 4.5 mm, which is the clearance size for an M4 (4 mm) screw, so the screw passes through freely. If you want an exact 4 mm hole instead, I can change it.

## How I oriented it: lying on its side
I drew the hook's side outline (back plate, arm and lip) flat on the plate and extruded it 25 mm upward:

- **Nothing overhangs.** Every wall is vertical. The arm and lip stand on the bed instead of sticking out into the air, which is what would need supports if the hook were printed upright against its back.
- **It's stronger this way.** Each layer contains the whole J shape. A coat pulls the arm down, and that load runs along the printed lines instead of trying to split layers apart, which is where printed hooks usually break.
- **It sits firmly.** About 830 mm² of the part touches the bed, and its centre of mass is low (12.5 mm up).
- **The screw holes print cleanly.** In this orientation they run sideways, so I made them teardrop-shaped (pointed at the top). That lets the top of each hole print without support.

## Checks
- **Full printability check:** "All checks passed." No problems with fitting on the plate, nozzle reach, holes in the mesh, overhangs, tipping or contact with the bed.
- **`measure`:** 0 mm² of overhang past 45°. The model is closed and is a single body.
- **I saved two checks with the project**, which rerun on every edit:
  - c1: overhang ≤ 0 mm², passes at 0 mm².
  - c2: thinnest wall at mid-width ≥ 1.6 mm, passes at 5.0 mm.
- **The holes really go through.** My first try only drilled 2.5 mm into the plate, which a horizontal cut through the middle of the part caught. After fixing it, the same cut splits the back plate into 3 separate pieces, with 4.5 mm gaps at 60 and 88 mm.

The project hasn't been saved to a file and I haven't sliced or printed anything yet. Two more things you could ask for: countersinks for flat-head screws, or a wider `gap` if the loop is thicker than 15 mm.
